## Careful - this is not the same as logging your data {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Back in **Vol 1**, when a relationship came out curved, we took logs of
the variables and fitted OLS to the transformed numbers. That also puts
a log in the model. **It is not the same thing**, and the difference is
worth ten minutes.

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**What we did in Vol 1 - log(lm)**

$$\log(y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + \epsilon_i$$

*Change the data, then model it.*

1.  Take every value of $y$ and log it
2.  Fit an ordinary regression to those new numbers
3.  You are now modelling the **average of the logged values**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**What a GLM does**

$$\log\big(E[y_i]\big) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i$$

*Model the data, and put the log on the model.*

1.  Leave every value of $y$ exactly as it is
2.  Work out its **average**, then log *that*
3.  You are modelling the **log of the average**
:::
:::::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
Read those two third points again. *Average of the logs* versus *log of
the average*. They sound like the same sentence in a different order.
:::

## The average of the logs is not the log of the average {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
fsm <- model_data$TFSM6CLA1A
fsm <- fsm[!is.na(fsm) & fsm > 0]
am  <- mean(fsm)
gm  <- exp(mean(log(fsm)))
```

It comes down to **which one you do first**. Take three schools, with 1, 10
and 100 disadvantaged pupils.

```{r}
#| label: toy-order
#| echo: false
toy  <- c(1, 10, 100)
t_gm <- exp(mean(log(toy)))
t_am <- mean(toy)
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**lm - Log first, then average**

*(what transforming the data does)*

1.  Log each one: `r paste(sprintf("%.2f", log(toy)), collapse = ", ")`
2.  Average those: `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(log(toy)))`
3.  Undo the log: **`r sprintf("%.0f", t_gm)`**
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**GLM - Average first, then log**

*(what a log link does)*

1.  Add them up and divide: **`r sprintf("%.0f", t_am)`**
2.  The model logs *that*:
    `r sprintf("%.2f", log(t_am))`
:::
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
Same three numbers. **`r sprintf("%.0f", t_gm)` against
`r sprintf("%.0f", t_am)`.** Nothing has gone wrong — the order of operations
simply matters, and $\log$ is the reason why.
:::

## The same thing, on our data {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

The **number of disadvantaged pupils** across our
`r comma(length(fsm))` schools:

| | What you do | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **LM - Log first, then average** | log each school, average, undo the log | **`r sprintf("%.1f", gm)`** pupils |
| **GLM - Average first, then log** | add them up and divide | **`r sprintf("%.1f", am)`** pupils |

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
-   **`r sprintf("%.1f", am - gm)` pupils apart — about
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (am - gm) / am)`.** Not a rounding error, and not a mistake in either calculation. They are answers to *different
questions*.
-   Logging first gives you the **geometric** mean. Whenever a
variable is skewed, it sits below the ordinary mean — and the more
skewed it is, the bigger the gap.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
-   A model fitted to logged data is not predicting the average number of disadvantaged pupils. 
-   It is predicting something smaller (geometric mean), and you have to remember to say so. **A log-link GLM predicts the average you actually meant.**
:::

## The same gap, inside a model {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| label: two-routes
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.1
#| fig-align: center

# Same scatter twice. Left: log the outcome, fit OLS, exponentiate back.
# Right: leave it alone, fit a Poisson GLM with a log link. Both put a log
# in the model; they do not predict the same thing.
tr <- model_data |>
  filter(!is.na(TPUP), !is.na(TFSM6CLA1A), TPUP > 0, TFSM6CLA1A > 0)

m_log <- lm(log(TFSM6CLA1A) ~ TPUP, data = tr)
m_glm <- glm(TFSM6CLA1A ~ TPUP, data = tr, family = poisson)

gr <- tibble(TPUP = seq(min(tr$TPUP), max(tr$TPUP), length.out = 250))
gr$log_route <- exp(predict(m_log, newdata = gr))
gr$glm_route <- predict(m_glm, newdata = gr, type = "response")

panel <- function(yvar, col, ttl, eqn) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_point(data = tr, aes(TPUP, TFSM6CLA1A),
               alpha = 0.10, colour = casa_purple, size = 0.7) +
    geom_line(data = gr, aes(TPUP, .data[[yvar]]), colour = col, linewidth = 1.3) +
    annotate("label", x = 15, y = 250, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 3.1,
             label = eqn, fill = "white", label.size = 0, colour = col) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 265)) +
    labs(title = ttl, x = "Pupils in the cohort", y = "Disadvantaged pupils") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10.5))
}

p_a <- panel("log_route", casa_red, "1. Log the data, fit OLS, convert back",
             sprintf("log(y) = %.2f + %.5f x\nthen y = exp(...)",
                     coef(m_log)[1], coef(m_log)[2]))
p_b <- panel("glm_route", casa_teal, "2. Leave the data, use a log link",
             sprintf("log(E[y]) = %.2f + %.5f x",
                     coef(m_glm)[1], coef(m_glm)[2]))

patchwork::wrap_plots(p_a, p_b, nrow = 1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
gap50 <- 100 * (predict(m_glm, data.frame(TPUP = 50), type = "response") -
                exp(predict(m_log, data.frame(TPUP = 50)))) /
         predict(m_glm, data.frame(TPUP = 50), type = "response")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
Same `r comma(nrow(tr))` schools, same predictor, both models with a log in
them — and **two different curves**. For a cohort of 50 the left-hand route
predicts about **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", gap50)` fewer** disadvantaged pupils than
the right-hand one. The two converge as schools get bigger, which is exactly
what you would expect: the more skewed the slice of data, the wider the gap.
:::

## So which one is right? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

For **counts, yes/no outcomes and proportions** this is not a matter of taste.
Logging is the wrong tool and a GLM is the right one.

For a **continuous, strictly positive** outcome both are defensible, and they
answer slightly different questions. Four things to ask:

::: incremental
1.  **What does the number have to do?** If it must *add up* — totals,
    budgets, headcounts — you need the arithmetic mean, so you need the GLM.
    **Geometric means do not aggregate.** Average logged predictions across
    150 LAs, convert back, and the total will be wrong
2.  **What type is the outcome?** Logging a count does not make it
    continuous. It makes it a logged discrete thing
3.  **Are there zeros?** Then there is no decision to make
4.  **What do you believe about the noise?** This is the real test, and it is
    checkable
:::

## It comes down to the errors {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Logging assumes** the error is **multiplicative** — roughly constant spread
on the log scale.

*A school is 20% above expectation, whatever its size.*
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**A log-link GLM assumes** the variance **grows with the mean**.

*Bigger schools vary more in absolute terms — which is what counts actually
do.*
:::
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
Plot the residuals against the fitted values. If the spread fans out on the
raw scale but is flat once logged, logging is honest. If the variance tracks
the mean, you want Poisson. **This is a question you can answer with a plot,
not a preference.**
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.84em;"}
**The published rule of thumb.** O'Hara & Kotze simulated count data and
compared the two approaches. Transformations performed poorly *except when
dispersion was small and the mean counts were large*; Poisson and negative
binomial models performed well throughout.

Which is exactly what the previous slide showed — `r sprintf("%.0f%%", gap50)`
apart at a cohort of 50, converging to almost nothing by 400. **Large counts,
small gap. Small counts, big gap.**
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.52em; color:#666; margin-top:0.4em;"}
O'Hara, R.B. & Kotze, D.J. (2010) Do not log-transform count data.
*Methods in Ecology and Evolution*, **1**(2), 118–122.
[doi:10.1111/j.2041-210X.2010.00021.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2041-210X.2010.00021.x)
:::

::: {.notes}
Reference: O'Hara, R.B. & Kotze, D.J. (2010) "Do not log-transform count
data", Methods in Ecology and Evolution 1(2): 118-122.
doi:10.1111/j.2041-210X.2010.00021.x

If a student asks for a one-line answer: the GLM is the safer default and for
counts it is the correct one. Logging is legitimate when the outcome is
continuous, positive, has no zeros, and the noise really is multiplicative -
and then it answers a question about the typical case rather than the average
case. If you cannot say which of those you want, you want the average, so use
the GLM.
:::

## And sometimes you cannot transform at all {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Even if you are happy with the geometric mean, transforming only works
if every value *can* be logged. Often they cannot.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
n_zero_fsm <- sum(model_data$TFSM6CLA1A == 0, na.rm = TRUE)

# The LA-level object `la` is not built until the Poisson section, so the
# same count is derived here rather than referenced forward.
n_zero_la <- schools |>
  group_by(LANAME) |>
  summarise(n_schools = n(), n_below = sum(below_good), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_schools >= 5, n_below == 0) |>
  nrow()
```

::: incremental
- **Zeros.** $\log(0)$ is $-\infty$. `r n_zero_fsm` of our schools have
  no disadvantaged pupils at all, and `r n_zero_la` local authorities
  have no below-Good schools. Every one of those rows drops out,
  silently
- **Yes/no outcomes.** A school is rated below Good or it is not. There
  is no scale to compress — $\log(0)$ and $\log(1)$ are $-\infty$ and
  $0$, and neither is any use
- **The usual bodge** is to log $y + 1$ instead. It works, and it
  quietly changes the thing you are modelling, by an amount that depends
  on how big your counts are
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:10px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.92em;"}
**A GLM never asks you to touch the data.** The zeros stay zeros, the 0s
and 1s stay 0s and 1s, and the link function does its work on the
*average* instead — where there is nothing awkward to divide by and
nothing to drop.
:::

## But hang on — what about the x variables? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

In **Vol 1** we did not just log the outcome. We logged the predictor too:

$$\log(y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log(x_i) + \epsilon_i$$

A Poisson GLM looks different. The log sits on the **left-hand side only**:

$$\log\big(E[y_i]\big) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$$

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**The link is a statement about the outcome's type.** Counts cannot go
negative, so we use a log link. That is *all* it says — and in particular it
says **nothing whatsoever about the predictors**.

You are still free to log them, or not, exactly as you always were. That
choice is untouched by the link, and we come to it next.
:::

## Logging a predictor is still available {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

It is just a **separate decision**, made for the same old reason — the
relationship is curved — and completely independent of the link.

```{r}
#| label: logged-predictor
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
la_x <- schools |>
  group_by(LANAME) |>
  summarise(n_below = sum(below_good), mean_abs = mean(PERCTOT, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_schools = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_schools >= 5, !is.na(mean_abs))
m_raw <- glm(n_below ~ mean_abs,      data = la_x, family = poisson)
m_log <- glm(n_below ~ log(mean_abs), data = la_x, family = poisson)
rr_raw <- exp(coef(m_raw)[2])
rr_dbl <- 2^coef(m_log)[2]
```

| | What goes in | How you read it |
|---|---|---|
| `n_below ~ mean_abs` | absence, raw | one **percentage point** more absence multiplies the rate by **`r sprintf("%.2f", rr_raw)`** |
| `n_below ~ log(mean_abs)` | absence, logged | **doubling** absence multiplies the rate by **`r sprintf("%.2f", rr_dbl)`** |

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
Both are Poisson models with a log link. Both leave the *outcome* untouched.
They differ only in whether the predictor enters raw or logged — and that
changes the sentence you write, from *per unit* to *per doubling*.

Here the logged version fits slightly better (AIC `r sprintf("%.0f", AIC(m_log))`
against `r sprintf("%.0f", AIC(m_raw))`), so it is a real choice, not a
formality.

[*AIC is a score for comparing models fitted to the same data — lower is
better. We take it apart properly later today.*]{style="font-size:0.85em; color:#666;"}
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:8px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.85em;"}
**One predictor we always log.** Later today we add `offset(log(n_schools))`
to account for how many schools an LA has. That is a logged predictor with its
coefficient *fixed at 1* — and it is what turns a model of counts into a model
of rates.
:::

## So should I log a skewed predictor? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Tempting, and a very common habit — but **not because it is skewed**.

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
Regression makes **no assumption whatsoever about the distribution of your
predictors**. The assumptions are about the *errors*. A skewed `x` breaks
nothing and is not, on its own, a problem to be fixed.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
Three things that **are** real reasons to log a predictor:

1.  **The relationship is curved.** Straightening it is the main reason, and
    the only one you can see on a scatter plot
2.  **A handful of extreme values are dragging the fit around.** Logging pulls
    in a long tail and reduces their leverage
3.  **You want a proportional reading** — *per 10% more* rather than *per unit
    more*
:::

## Skew does not predict whether logging helps {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| label: skew-vs-logging
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
sv <- model_data |>
  drop_na(TPUP, TFSM6CLA1A, PTFSM6CLA1A, PTEALGRP2) |>
  filter(if_all(c(TPUP, PTFSM6CLA1A, PTEALGRP2), ~ .x > 0))
skw <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3

tibble(
  Predictor = c("Pupils in the cohort", "% disadvantaged",
                "% English as an additional language"),
  var = c("TPUP", "PTFSM6CLA1A", "PTEALGRP2")
) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    Skew = sprintf("%.2f", skw(sv[[var]])),
    a = AIC(glm(reformulate(var, "TFSM6CLA1A"), data = sv, family = poisson)),
    b = AIC(glm(reformulate(sprintf("log(%s)", var), "TFSM6CLA1A"),
                data = sv, family = poisson)),
    `Does logging help?` = if (b < a - 2) "Yes, clearly"
                           else if (b > a + 2) "No - it makes it worse"
                           else "No real difference"
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(Predictor, Skew, `Does logging help?`) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrl")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
The **least** skewed predictor here is one where logging clearly helps. The
**most** skewed is the one where logging actively makes the model worse.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
**Look at the relationship, not at the histogram of x.** Skew in a predictor
tells you how its values are spread out. It tells you nothing at all about
whether its relationship with the outcome is straight — and that is the thing
you are actually trying to fix.
:::

## So how do you tell? Draw it twice {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| label: straighter-which-way
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| fig-align: center

# Outcome on a log axis, because that is the scale a log-link model works on.
# Straight on this plot = straight on the link scale. Dashed line is the
# straight-line fit; solid curve is a loess smoother following the data.
sv2 <- sv |> filter(TFSM6CLA1A > 0)

# Binned averages rather than a loess curve. With 3,000 points and a lot of
# tied low values, loess spikes badly at the left-hand edge; binning is both
# steadier and a technique the students can use themselves.
draw <- function(xv, logx, lab) {
  dat <- sv2 |>
    mutate(xval = if (logx) log10(.data[[xv]]) else .data[[xv]],
           bin  = ntile(xval, 18)) |>
    group_by(bin) |>
    summarise(x = mean(xval), y = exp(mean(log(TFSM6CLA1A))), .groups = "drop")

  ggplot(dat, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
                colour = casa_red, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_line(colour = casa_teal, linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(colour = casa_teal, size = 1.8) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    labs(title = lab, x = NULL, y = "Disadvantaged pupils") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 9.5))
}

patchwork::wrap_plots(
  draw("PTFSM6CLA1A", FALSE, "% disadvantaged — raw"),
  draw("PTFSM6CLA1A", TRUE,  "% disadvantaged — logged"),
  draw("PTEALGRP2",   FALSE, "% EAL — raw"),
  draw("PTEALGRP2",   TRUE,  "% EAL — logged"),
  nrow = 2)
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.78em"}
Schools split into 18 equal groups along the x-axis; each **teal dot** is one
group's average. **Dashed** is the straight line the model would fit. Where
the dots wander away from the dashed line, the relationship is curved.
:::

## The tip worth remembering {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Plot your outcome against the predictor twice — once raw, once logged — and
keep whichever is straighter.**

Put the outcome on a **log axis** while you do it, because that is the scale a
log-link model actually works on. Straight on that plot means straight where
the model cares.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
On the previous slide, look at the **top row**: raw, the dots curve away from
the line; logged, they drop neatly onto it. That is a predictor worth logging,
and you can see it before fitting anything.

The **bottom row** does not improve. Logging the EAL figures just moves the
scatter around — which is exactly why the AIC got *worse* when we logged it.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.84em;"}
**Three habits that will serve you all term**

1.  Draw it before you model it — curvature is obvious in a picture and
    invisible in a coefficient
2.  Add a **smoother** alongside the straight line. If they agree, a straight
    line is fine; if they diverge, you have found something
3.  If logging a predictor does not visibly straighten anything, **leave it
    alone**. A transformation you cannot justify is one more thing to explain
    in your write-up
:::

# Can we predict School Ofsted ratings? {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Our question for today {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- We have used Ofsted ratings as a **predictor** and as a **grouping
  variable** already
- Today we turn it around and make it the **outcome**
- *Given everything else we know about a school - its results, its
  intake, its absence rates, its size - can we predict what Ofsted said
  about it?*
- And if we can, what does that tell us about what Ofsted is actually
  measuring?
- **Note**, *Ofsted has changed how it rates schools now, so single-word ratings are no longer given*

## The outcome variable {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| out-width: 95%

model_data |>
  count(rating4) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rating4, y = n, fill = rating4)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma(n)), vjust = -0.4, size = 5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(casa_red, casa_pink, casa_teal, casa_green)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Schools",
       title = "Ofsted ratings, mainstream secondaries in England") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
`r comma(nrow(model_data))` schools with complete data. Note immediately
how **lopsided** this is - we will come back to that, because it causes
more trouble than anything else today.
:::

## First attempt: just use OLS? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- Let's re-code our ratings: "below Good" as **1** and "Good or better"
  as **0**
- We can regress it on Progress 8 exactly as we have been doing for the
  last three weeks.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
lpm <- lm(below_good ~ P8MEA, data = model_data)
summary(lpm)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
lpm_range <- range(fitted(lpm))
lpm_neg   <- sum(fitted(lpm) < 0)
# What the straight line predicts for a solidly above-average school, used in
# the caption on the next slide. Computed rather than typed so it cannot drift
# if the filters on model_data ever change.
p8_one    <- as.numeric(predict(lpm, newdata = data.frame(P8MEA = 1)))
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
The model runs. It produces coefficients. It produces an R². Nothing
errors.

**And its fitted values run from `r round(lpm_range[1], 3)` to
`r round(lpm_range[2], 3)`.**
:::

## A probability of minus fifty percent? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| out-width: 95%

grid <- tibble(P8MEA = seq(min(model_data$P8MEA), max(model_data$P8MEA), length.out = 300))
grid$lpm <- predict(lpm, newdata = grid)
glm1 <- glm(below_good ~ P8MEA, data = model_data, family = binomial)
grid$glm <- predict(glm1, newdata = grid, type = "response")

ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 1, ymax = Inf,
           fill = casa_red, alpha = 0.08) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = 0,
           fill = casa_red, alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_jitter(data = model_data, aes(P8MEA, below_good),
              height = 0.03, alpha = 0.10, colour = casa_purple, size = 0.9) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(P8MEA, lpm, colour = "Straight line (OLS)"), linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(P8MEA, glm, colour = "Logistic curve"), linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  # Mark the single point the caption talks about, so it can be found on the
  # graph rather than taken on trust
  annotate("point", x = 1, y = p8_one, colour = casa_red, size = 3.2) +
  annotate("segment", x = 1, xend = 1.45, y = p8_one, yend = p8_one - 0.18,
           colour = casa_red, linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = p8_one - 0.21, hjust = 0, size = 4,
           colour = casa_red,
           label = sprintf("Progress 8 = +1\npredicts %.0f%%", 100 * p8_one)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Straight line (OLS)" = casa_red,
                                 "Logistic curve" = casa_teal), name = NULL) +
  # The caption talks in percentages, so the axis does too - a probability
  # axis labelled 0.00-1.00 against a caption saying "-13%" invites exactly
  # the question of where the -13% is supposed to be
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(x = "Progress 8 score", y = "P(rated below Good)",
       title = "The shaded bands are impossible probabilities") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
- The straight line gives **`r comma(lpm_neg)` schools a negative
  probability** of being rated below good.
- At a Progress 8 of +1 it predicts a probability of being rated below
  good of about **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * p8_one)`** (impossible).
- The logistic curve cannot do this - it is bounded at 0 and 1 by
  construction.
:::

## Where the curve comes from {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

We need something that takes a straight line, which runs from $-\infty$
to $+\infty$, and squashes it into $[0,1]$.

::: incremental
- Start with the **probability** $p$ - bounded at 0 and 1, e.g. 0.4
  (40%), awkward
- Turn it into **odds**,
  $\frac{p}{1-p} = \frac{probability of happening}{probability of NOT happening}$
  or $\frac{0.4}{0.6} = 0.67$ - now bounded at 0 and $+\infty$, better
- Take the **log** of that
  ($\log\left(\frac{0.4}{0.6}\right) = -0.40$) - now unbounded in both
  directions :tada:
:::

. . .

$$\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots$$

- That left-hand side is the **logit**, and it ***is*** the link
  function. The right-hand side is exactly the model we have been
  fitting since week 5.
- A **logit** simply is a mathematical function that converts a
  probability (between 0 and 1) into a log-odds value that can range
  from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$
- The link-function converts the expected value of the outcome (the
  mean) into something a straight line can cope with

## Odds are not probabilities {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Worth pausing, because this trips people (including me!) up all the
time.

| Probability | Odds | In words            |
|-------------|------|---------------------|
| 0.5         | 1.0  | Evens               |
| 0.75        | 3.0  | Three to one on     |
| 0.9         | 9.0  | Nine to one on      |
| 0.1         | 0.11 | Nine to one against |

. . .

Probabilities are bounded above. **Odds are not.** That is the whole
reason we work with them.

## And odds are not odds *ratios* {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Odds** describe **one** situation

$$\text{odds} = \frac{p}{1-p}$$

*"This school's odds of being rated below Good are 0.10"*
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
**An odds ratio** compares **two**

$$\text{OR} = \frac{\text{odds}_A}{\text{odds}_B}$$

*"...which is 0.07 times the odds of a school one Progress 8 point
worse"*
:::
:::::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
- Easily the most common mistake in reading logistic output.
- The odds are the raw ingredient;
- the **ratio** is what you get when you put two of them side by side -
  and the **odds-ratio** is what a regression coefficient hands you.
:::

## Why the coefficient *is* a ratio {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

**First, where the "one" comes from.** A slope always answers the same
question, in every model you have ever fitted:

> *If the predictor goes up by **one unit**, what happens to the outcome?*

In Vol 1 that was *"one more percentage point of absence costs 0.38 Attainment
8 points"*. The **one** is not special — it is just the step size we have
always quoted coefficients in.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
So picture **two schools, identical in every respect**, except the second has
one more unit of $x$ — one more percentage point of absence, say.
:::

## Why the coefficient *is* a ratio {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Our model says the log-odds are a straight line:

$$\log(\text{odds}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
| | Predictor | Its log-odds |
|---|---|---|
| **School A** | $x$ | $\beta_0 + \beta_1x$ |
| **School B** | $x+1$ | $\beta_0 + \beta_1x + \beta_1$ |
:::

. . .

Subtract one from the other, and everything cancels except $\beta_1$:

$$\log(\text{odds}_B) - \log(\text{odds}_A) = \beta_1$$

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
**So the coefficient is a difference of two log-odds.** Not a difference in
probability, and not a difference in odds — a difference in *logged* odds.
:::

## From a difference to a ratio {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

We have a **difference of logs**. There is a rule from school algebra for
exactly that:

$$\log(M) - \log(N) = \log\!\left(\frac{M}{N}\right)$$

[Deliberately *not* A and B — those are taken. $M$ and $N$ are just
placeholders for "whatever you are subtracting".]{style="font-size:0.8em; color:#666;"}

. . .

Ours was $\log(\text{odds}_B) - \log(\text{odds}_A)$, so $M$ is **School B's**
odds and $N$ is **School A's**:

$$\beta_1 = \log(\text{odds}_B) - \log(\text{odds}_A) = \log\!\left(\frac{\text{odds}_B}{\text{odds}_A}\right)$$

. . .

Now undo the log on both sides — exponentiate:

$$e^{\beta_1} = \frac{\text{odds}_B}{\text{odds}_A}$$

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.9em;"}
**That is the whole thing.** A ratio of two odds — because subtracting logs
*is* dividing, and the coefficient was a difference of logs all along. Nothing
was smuggled in: just a one-unit step, and one rule about logarithms.
:::

## See it in our own data {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Single-predictor model, so the arithmetic is visible. glm1 is already fitted
# on the "minus fifty percent" slide.
odds_at <- function(x) {
  p <- predict(glm1, newdata = data.frame(P8MEA = x), type = "response")
  as.numeric(p / (1 - p))
}
b1 <- as.numeric(coef(glm1)["P8MEA"])

tibble(
  `Progress 8`  = c(-1, 0, 1, 2),
  Probability   = sprintf("%.3f", map_dbl(c(-1, 0, 1, 2),
                    ~ as.numeric(predict(glm1, data.frame(P8MEA = .x), type = "response")))),
  Odds          = sprintf("%.4f", map_dbl(c(-1, 0, 1, 2), odds_at)),
  `Odds ÷ the row above` = c("-", sprintf("%.3f", map_dbl(c(0, 1, 2),
                    ~ odds_at(.x) / odds_at(.x - 1))))
) |> kable(align = "rrrr")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.86em"}
**Where each column comes from.** The **probability** is simply what the model
predicts at that Progress 8 score. The **odds** is that probability converted
with $p \div (1-p)$ — at Progress 8 of 0 the model says
`r sprintf("%.3f", as.numeric(predict(glm1, data.frame(P8MEA=0), type="response")))`,
so the odds are that divided by one minus itself =
**`r sprintf("%.4f", odds_at(0))`**. The last column divides each row's odds by
the one above it.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
The coefficient on Progress 8 is **`r sprintf("%.2f", b1)`**, and
$e^{`r sprintf("%.2f", b1)`}$ = **`r sprintf("%.3f", exp(b1))`**.

That is the last column, every time. **One coefficient, one odds ratio,
valid wherever you start from.** Now look at the probabilities - they
fall
`r sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(predict(glm1, data.frame(P8MEA=-1), type="response")))`
→
`r sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(predict(glm1, data.frame(P8MEA=0), type="response")))`
→
`r sprintf("%.3f", as.numeric(predict(glm1, data.frame(P8MEA=1), type="response")))`,
doing nothing so tidy. Which is exactly why *"the probability falls by
X"* is never a safe reading of a logistic coefficient.
:::

# Binary logistic regression {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Running the model {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Same formula interface you have used for three weeks. Two differences:
`glm()` not `lm()`, and a `family` argument.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
logit_below <- glm(
  below_good ~ P8MEA + PTFSM6CLA1A + PERCTOT + PPERSABS10 +
               log(TPUP) + PTPRIORHI + MINORGROUP,
  data   = train,
  family = binomial
)
```

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
ct <- summary(logit_below)$coefficients
tibble(
  Term        = rownames(ct),
  Coefficient = round(ct[, 1], 3),
  `Std. error`= round(ct[, 2], 3),
  `p`         = ifelse(ct[, 4] < 0.001, "<0.001", as.character(round(ct[, 4], 3)))
) |> kable()
```

## These coefficients are on the log-odds scale {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- A coefficient of `r round(coef(logit_below)["P8MEA"], 2)` on Progress
  8 does **not** mean "the probability falls by
  `r abs(round(coef(logit_below)["P8MEA"], 2))`"
- It means the **log-odds** fall by that much, for every one-point
  increase in Progress 8
- Nobody thinks in log-odds. So we exponentiate, and get an **odds
  ratio**

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: true
exp(coef(logit_below)["P8MEA"])
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
**One extra Progress 8 point multiplies the odds of being rated below
Good by about `r round(exp(coef(logit_below)["P8MEA"]), 2)`** - that is,
it cuts them by roughly
`r round(100 * (1 - exp(coef(logit_below)["P8MEA"])))`%.
:::

## Reading odds ratios {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| out-width: 92%

or_tbl <- tibble(
  term = names(coef(logit_below)),
  est  = coef(logit_below),
  se   = summary(logit_below)$coefficients[, 2]
) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(or = exp(est), lo = exp(est - 1.96 * se), hi = exp(est + 1.96 * se),
         term = recode(term,
           "P8MEA" = "Progress 8",
           "PTFSM6CLA1A" = "% disadvantaged",
           "PERCTOT" = "% overall absence",
           "PPERSABS10" = "% persistently absent",
           "log(TPUP)" = "log(cohort size)",
           "PTPRIORHI" = "% high prior attainers",
           "MINORGROUPMaintained school" = "Maintained (vs academy)"))

ggplot(or_tbl, aes(x = or, y = fct_reorder(term, or))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = casa_red, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.25, colour = casa_purple) +
  geom_point(size = 3.4, colour = casa_teal) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Odds ratio (log scale)", y = NULL,
       title = "Odds of being rated below Good",
       subtitle = "Left of the dashed line = protective; right = raises the odds")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
Anything whose interval crosses **1** is doing nothing detectable. Note
how much work Progress 8 is doing compared with everything else.
:::

## How do you score a model like this? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

For three weeks we judged models with **R²** — the share of the variation in
the outcome the model managed to explain.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
That worked because the outcome was a *number*, with variation in it to
explain. Ours is a **yes or no**. There is no spread to account for, and R²
as you know it simply does not exist here.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
So we ask **two** questions instead, and they are genuinely different:

1.  **Does the model fit the data?** — likelihood, deviance, AIC, the
    pseudo-R²s, Hosmer–Lemeshow
2.  **Does it make good decisions?** — accuracy, the confusion matrix, ROC
    and AUC

A model can do respectably on one and badly on the other. We take them in
turn.
:::

# 1. Does the model fit? {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Likelihood: how surprised is the model? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| label: fit-stats
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
n_tr   <- nrow(train)
ll     <- as.numeric(logLik(logit_below))
dev0   <- logit_below$null.deviance
dev1   <- logit_below$deviance
k      <- length(coef(logit_below))
cs     <- 1 - exp((dev1 - dev0) / n_tr)
cs_max <- 1 - exp(-dev0 / n_tr)
nk     <- cs / cs_max
```

Every school in the data either was or was not rated below Good. The model
assigns each one a probability. **Likelihood** asks the obvious question:

> *Given these coefficients, how probable was the data we actually saw?*

::: incremental
-   A school that *was* below Good, which the model gave 0.9 — good, that was
    likely
-   A school that was **not**, which the model gave 0.9 — bad, the model was
    confidently wrong
-   Multiply all `r comma(n_tr)` of those probabilities together and you have
    the **likelihood** of the whole dataset
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
Fitting the model *is* choosing the coefficients that make this number as
large as possible — **maximum likelihood**. We report its log, because
multiplying `r comma(n_tr)` probabilities together gives a number too small
for a computer to hold.

For our model: **log-likelihood = `r sprintf("%.1f", ll)`**. Always negative;
closer to zero is better.
:::

## Deviance: distance from a perfect fit {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

A log-likelihood on its own is hard to read. **Deviance** rescales it into
something more like an error score — *how far this model sits from one that
predicted every school perfectly*.

$$\text{deviance} = -2 \times \text{log-likelihood}$$

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
| | | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **Null deviance** | `r sprintf("%.1f", dev0)` | with **no predictors at all** — just the overall rate |
| **Residual deviance** | `r sprintf("%.1f", dev1)` | with our seven predictors in |
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Lower is better**, and the drop — `r sprintf("%.0f", dev0 - dev1)` — is what
the predictors bought us. This is the direct equivalent of the sum-of-squares
drop you used to read off an OLS table.
:::

::: {.notes}
Deviance is also the statistic behind the overdispersion check later in the
Poisson section: residual deviance divided by residual degrees of freedom.
Worth flagging forward so it is not a surprise there.
:::

## AIC: fit, minus a fine for complexity {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

There is a problem with judging a model on deviance alone: **adding any
predictor, however useless, will always lower it slightly.** Left to itself,
deviance always says "more variables".

. . .

So we charge for them:

$$\text{AIC} = \text{deviance} + 2k \quad\text{where } k = \text{number of coefficients}$$

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
For our model: `r sprintf("%.1f", dev1)` + 2 × `r k` =
**`r sprintf("%.1f", dev1 + 2*k)`**. A predictor only improves the AIC if it
reduces the deviance by more than the 2 points it costs.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
**AIC has no meaning on its own.** `r sprintf("%.0f", AIC(logit_below))` is
neither good nor bad — it is only useful for **comparing models fitted to the
same data**. Lower wins. That is exactly how we used it earlier to choose
between a raw and a logged predictor.
:::

## The pseudo-R²s {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

People badly want an R², so several substitutes exist. The two you will meet
in software output:

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Cox & Snell** — built from the likelihood ratio between your model and the
null model. For us: **`r sprintf("%.3f", cs)`**.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
That looks dismal — until you learn its catch. **Cox & Snell cannot reach 1.**
With a binary outcome its ceiling here is **`r sprintf("%.3f", cs_max)`**, so
`r sprintf("%.3f", cs)` is really `r sprintf("%.3f", cs)` out of a possible
`r sprintf("%.3f", cs_max)`.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Nagelkerke** fixes precisely that, by dividing by the ceiling:

$$R^2_{\text{Nagelkerke}} = \frac{`r sprintf("%.3f", cs)`}{`r sprintf("%.3f", cs_max)`} = \mathbf{`r sprintf("%.3f", nk)`}$$

Now it can reach 1, and it reads much more like the R² you are used to.
:::

## ...and how much to trust them {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
Report them if the journal or the marker expects them — but know what you are
saying.

::: incremental
-   **They are not "variance explained".** Nothing here is variance. The name
    is borrowed, and the interpretation does not come with it
-   **They are not comparable across datasets**, and barely across models. A
    Nagelkerke of 0.32 is not "half as good" as one of 0.64
-   **There is no accepted threshold** for a good one. Values that would be
    embarrassing in OLS are routine here
:::
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
Treat a pseudo-R² as a **rough indication that the predictors are doing
something**, and nothing more. If you want to know whether the model is
actually any use, ask the second question — the one we come to next.
:::

## Hosmer–Lemeshow: does it fit everywhere? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| label: hoslem
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
pfit <- fitted(logit_below)
hl_g <- 10
hl_grp <- cut(pfit, breaks = quantile(pfit, probs = seq(0, 1, 1/hl_g)),
              include.lowest = TRUE)
hl_obs <- tapply(train$below_good, hl_grp, sum)
hl_exp <- tapply(pfit, hl_grp, sum)
hl_n   <- tapply(pfit, hl_grp, length)
hl_chi <- sum((hl_obs - hl_exp)^2 / (hl_exp * (1 - hl_exp / hl_n)))
hl_p   <- pchisq(hl_chi, hl_g - 2, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

Everything so far gives one number for the whole model. **Hosmer–Lemeshow**
asks something more specific: *is the model well calibrated across the whole
range of risk, or only in parts of it?*

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
1.  Sort the schools by predicted probability and cut them into **10 equal
    groups**
2.  In each group, compare **how many actually were** below Good with **how
    many the model expected**
3.  Add up the discrepancies into a chi-squared statistic
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
Ours: $\chi^2$ = **`r sprintf("%.1f", hl_chi)`** on `r hl_g - 2` df,
**p = `r sprintf("%.3f", hl_p)`**.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.84em;"}
**Read the direction carefully — it is the opposite of most tests.** A
*small* p-value means the model fits **badly**. Ours is
`r sprintf("%.2f", hl_p)`, so there is no evidence of poor fit.

And "no evidence of poor fit" is **not** the same as "good fit". The test is
known to be sensitive to how many groups you choose, and to have little power
on small samples. It is a flag worth checking, not a certificate.
:::

# 2. Does it make good decisions? {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Don't mark your own homework {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

The obvious way to answer that is to run the model over our schools and count
how often it got the answer right.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**The problem: it has already seen those schools.** The coefficients were
chosen to fit them as closely as possible. Scoring a model on the data it was
fitted to is revising with the exam paper in front of you — you will do well,
and it tells you nothing about the next paper.
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# Split the schools in two, before fitting anything
set.seed(42)
train_idx <- sample(nrow(model_data), floor(0.7 * nrow(model_data)))
train <- model_data[train_idx, ]   # fit the model on these
test  <- model_data[-train_idx, ]  # judge it on these
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
`r comma(nrow(train))` schools to **learn** from, `r comma(nrow(test))` kept
back to **test** on. The model never sees the second group while it is being
fitted, so how it does there is a fair sitting of a fresh paper.

That is what **test-set accuracy** means: of the `r comma(nrow(test))` schools
it had never met, what share did it classify correctly?
:::

## So how good is it? {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
p_below <- predict(logit_below, newdata = test, type = "response")
accuracy <- mean((p_below > 0.5) == test$below_good)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
baseline <- max(mean(test$below_good), 1 - mean(test$below_good))
auc_below <- auc_of(p_below, test$below_good)
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em"}
**Test-set accuracy: `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * accuracy)`**
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em"}
Not bad! Nearly nine schools in ten classified correctly.
:::

. . .

::: {.fragment style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #C94C4C"}
**Now watch.**
:::

## The single most important slide today {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: 90%

tibble(
  model = c("Our logistic model", "A model that always\nsays 'not below Good'"),
  acc   = c(accuracy, baseline)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_rev(model), y = 100 * acc, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * acc)), hjust = -0.15, size = 6) +
  coord_flip(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(casa_teal, casa_red)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Test-set accuracy (%)",
       title = "Our model versus a model that does nothing at all") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
A model that makes **the same prediction every single time**, with no
data at all, scores `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * baseline)`. Our model
beats it by **`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (accuracy - baseline))`
percentage points**.
:::

## Why accuracy lied to us {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
cm <- table(Actual = ifelse(test$below_good == 1, "Below Good", "Good or better"),
            Predicted = ifelse(p_below > 0.5, "Below Good", "Good or better"))

# kable() silently drops the dimnames of a table object, which leaves the
# reader with two identical sets of labels and no way to tell which axis is
# which. Rebuilt as a data frame so the headings say so explicitly.
tibble::tibble(
  ` ` = paste("**Actually**", rownames(cm)),
  `Predicted below Good`     = as.integer(cm[, "Below Good"]),
  `Predicted Good or better` = as.integer(cm[, "Good or better"])
) |>
  kable(align = "lrr")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em"}
The `r comma(nrow(test))` **test** schools — the ones the model never saw
while it was being fitted.
:::

::: incremental
- Only **`r comma(sum(test$below_good))`** of the `r comma(nrow(test))`
  test schools are actually below Good - the class is **rare**
- The model catches **`r cm["Below Good", "Below Good"]`** of them and
  misses **`r cm["Below Good", "Good or better"]`**
- If you were Ofsted, trying to decide which schools to visit, this
  model would be close to useless *at this threshold*
:::

. . .

**Always, always compare your accuracy against the majority-class
baseline.** On imbalanced data, accuracy on its own is not evidence of
anything.

## 0.5 was a choice, not a law {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

The model does not output yes or no. It outputs a **probability** for every
school. We turned that into a yes/no by flagging anything above **0.5** — and
nothing made 0.5 the right number.

```{r}
#| label: threshold-table
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
thr_tbl <- map_dfr(c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1), function(t) {
  flag <- p_below > t
  tibble(`Flag if probability above` = sprintf("%.2f", t),
         `Struggling schools caught`  = sum(flag & test$below_good == 1),
         `...and missed`              = sum(!flag & test$below_good == 1),
         `False alarms`               = sum(flag & test$below_good == 0))
})
kable(thr_tbl, align = "crrr")
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
Drop the threshold and you catch far more struggling schools — **32 up to
121** of the `r comma(sum(test$below_good))`. But the false alarms go from
**23 to 316**.

**There is no setting that is simply best.** Which error hurts more is a
policy question, and the model cannot answer it for you.
:::

## Every threshold at once: the ROC curve {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Rather than argue about one cut-off, plot **all of them**. Two numbers per
threshold:

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
- **True positive rate** — of the schools that *really are* below Good, what
  share did we flag? *(we want this high)*
- **False positive rate** — of the schools that are *fine*, what share did we
  flag anyway? *(we want this low)*
:::

```{r}
#| label: roc-explained
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-align: center
thr_all <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 400)
roc_df <- map_dfr(thr_all, function(t) {
  tibble(tpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 1] > t),
         fpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 0] > t))
})
marks <- map_dfr(c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1), function(t) {
  tibble(t = t,
         tpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 1] > t),
         fpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 0] > t))
})

ggplot(roc_df, aes(fpr, tpr)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(colour = casa_teal, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = marks, colour = casa_red, size = 2.6) +
  geom_text(data = marks, aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", t)),
            hjust = -0.35, size = 3.2, colour = casa_red) +
  labs(x = "False positive rate", y = "True positive rate") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
**Each red dot is one row of the table above.** Sweep the threshold from 1
down to 0 and you trace the whole curve. The dashed diagonal is what you would
get by **guessing at random** — the further above it you sit, the more the
model knows.
:::

## And AUC is the area underneath it {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
One curve is awkward to quote in a sentence, so we summarise it by the **area
under it** — the *AUC*.
:::

| AUC | What it means |
|---|---|
| **0.5** | the diagonal — no better than tossing a coin |
| **0.7–0.8** | useful |
| **0.9+** | very strong |
| **1.0** | perfect: every struggling school scored above every healthy one |

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
It also has a reading that needs no curve at all:

> **Pick one struggling school and one healthy school at random. AUC is the
> probability the model gives the struggling one the higher score.**
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.88em;"}
Notice what that does **not** depend on: any threshold. AUC asks whether the
model puts schools in the right **order**, which is a different and fairer
question from whether it labels them correctly at one arbitrary cut-off.
:::

## But the model is not useless {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Accuracy asks "did you get it right?" at one arbitrary cut-off. A better
question is "**do you rank schools sensibly?**"

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: 95%

thr <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 300)
roc <- map_dfr(thr, function(t) {
  tibble(tpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 1] > t),
         fpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 0] > t))
})

p_roc <- ggplot(roc, aes(fpr, tpr)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(colour = casa_teal, linewidth = 1.3) +
  labs(x = "False positive rate", y = "True positive rate",
       title = sprintf("ROC curve - AUC = %.3f", auc_below))

p_box <- tibble(p = p_below,
                actual = ifelse(test$below_good == 1, "Below Good", "Good or better")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = actual, y = p, fill = actual)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.75, outlier.alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = casa_red) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(casa_pink, casa_teal)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Predicted probability",
       title = "Predictions, by what actually happened") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_roc + p_box
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
**AUC = `r sprintf("%.3f", auc_below)`** - pick a below-Good school and
a Good-or-better school at random, and the model gives the below-Good
one a higher score `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * auc_below)` of the time.
That is genuinely useful. The problem was never the model - it was the
**0.5 threshold**, which is a choice, not a law.
:::

## Moving the threshold {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: 95%

sweep <- map_dfr(seq(0.02, 0.9, by = 0.01), function(t) {
  pred <- p_below > t
  tibble(threshold = t,
         `Caught (recall)`   = mean(pred[test$below_good == 1]),
         `Correct when flagged (precision)` =
            ifelse(sum(pred) == 0, NA, mean(test$below_good[pred] == 1)))
}) |>
  pivot_longer(-threshold)

ggplot(sweep, aes(threshold, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(casa_purple, casa_teal), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Classification threshold", y = NULL,
       title = "There is no free lunch here") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
Drop the threshold and you catch more struggling schools, but more of
your flags are false alarms. **Which error is worse is a policy
question, not a statistical one** - and that is the right way round.
:::

## A second outcome, same story {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
logit_out <- glm(
  outstanding ~ P8MEA + PTFSM6CLA1A + PERCTOT + PPERSABS10 +
                log(TPUP) + PTPRIORHI + MINORGROUP,
  data = train, family = binomial)
p_out <- predict(logit_out, newdata = test, type = "response")
acc_out <- mean((p_out > 0.5) == test$outstanding)
base_out <- max(mean(test$outstanding), 1 - mean(test$outstanding))
auc_out <- auc_of(p_out, test$outstanding)

tibble(
  Model = c("Below Good vs Good+", "Outstanding vs rest"),
  Accuracy = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * c(accuracy, acc_out)),
  Baseline = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * c(baseline, base_out)),
  AUC = sprintf("%.3f", c(auc_below, auc_out)),
  `Caught at p > 0.5` = c(
    sprintf("%d of %d", cm["Below Good", "Below Good"], sum(test$below_good)),
    sprintf("%d of %d", sum(p_out > 0.5 & test$outstanding == 1), sum(test$outstanding)))
) |> kable()
```

. . .

- Higher AUC, so the ranking is even better
- Barely above baseline on accuracy, and still catching well under half
  the Outstanding schools
- **Not a quirk of one model.** This is what rare outcomes do, and you
  will meet it in your own data

## An uncomfortable question {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Progress 8 is by far the strongest predictor in both models. So what
have we actually built?

::: incremental
- Ofsted inspectors **read a school's Progress 8 score before they
  visit**
- So we are not independently predicting a judgement - we are partly
  **recovering one of Ofsted's own inputs**
- That is circularity, and it makes the model much less interesting than
  it first looked
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
And a second problem: inspection dates in this file run from
**`r min(model_data$insp_year, na.rm = TRUE)` to
`r max(model_data$insp_year, na.rm = TRUE)`**, median
`r median(model_data$insp_year, na.rm = TRUE)`. Some of these ratings
were handed out a decade before the results we are using to "predict"
them.

**Ask these questions of your own models.** They matter more than
another decimal place of AUC.
:::

# Categories with an order {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## We threw information away {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- To fit a binary model, we collapsed four ratings into two
- But Ofsted ratings have an obvious **order**: Inadequate \< Requires
  improvement \< Good \< Outstanding
- Treating them as a number (1, 2, 3, 4) is the mistake we warned about
  in week 1 - it assumes the gaps are equal
- Treating them as unordered throws away real information

. . .

**Ordinal logistic regression** uses the order without assuming the
spacing.

## The idea: cut points on a hidden scale {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: 95%

ord <- polr(
  rating4 ~ P8MEA + PTFSM6CLA1A + PERCTOT + PPERSABS10 +
            log(TPUP) + PTPRIORHI + MINORGROUP,
  data = train, Hess = TRUE)
cuts <- ord$zeta

x <- seq(-9, 7, length.out = 600)
tibble(x = x, y = dlogis(x)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(fill = casa_teal, alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(colour = casa_teal, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cuts, colour = casa_red, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = c(-7.5, -4.3, -0.5, 4.5), y = 0.27,
           label = c("Inadequate", "Requires\nimprovement", "Good", "Outstanding"),
           size = 4.6, colour = casa_purple) +
  annotate("text", x = cuts, y = 0.02, label = sprintf("%.2f", cuts),
           size = 3.6, colour = casa_red, vjust = -0.3) +
  labs(x = "Latent 'school quality' scale", y = NULL,
       title = "One underlying scale, three estimated cut points") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
We imagine a single continuous scale we cannot observe. The predictors
move a school along it, and the **cut points** decide which rating it
comes out as. Three cut points for four categories - and the model
estimates them from the data rather than assuming them.
:::

## Running it {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(MASS)
ord <- polr(
  rating4 ~ P8MEA + PTFSM6CLA1A + PERCTOT + PPERSABS10 +
            log(TPUP) + PTPRIORHI + MINORGROUP,
  data = train, Hess = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
oc <- coef(summary(ord))
op <- 2 * pnorm(abs(oc[, 3]), lower.tail = FALSE)
tibble(
  Term  = rownames(oc),
  Value = round(oc[, 1], 3),
  `t`   = round(oc[, 3], 2),
  `p`   = ifelse(op < 0.001, "<0.001", as.character(round(op, 3)))
) |> kable()
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
The last three rows are the cut points, not predictors. Everything above
them reads like a logistic model: positive means *more likely to be
rated higher*.
:::

## Did it work? {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
pred_ord <- predict(ord, newdata = test)
acc_ord  <- mean(as.character(pred_ord) == as.character(test$rating4))
base_ord <- max(prop.table(table(test$rating4)))
within1  <- mean(abs(as.integer(pred_ord) - as.integer(test$rating4)) <= 1)
cm_ord   <- table(Actual = test$rating4, Predicted = pred_ord)
kable(cm_ord)
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
- Accuracy **`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * acc_ord)`** against a baseline
  of `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * base_ord)`
- It **never once** correctly predicts Inadequate -
  `r cm_ord["Inadequate", "Inadequate"]` out of
  `r sum(cm_ord["Inadequate", ])`
- But it is within one category **`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * within1)`**
  of the time
:::

## So: can we predict Ofsted? {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em"}
**Roughly, yes. Precisely, no. And the rare categories, not at all.**
:::

. . .

- The model knows the difference between a likely-Outstanding school and
  a likely-struggling one
- It cannot tell you which side of a single grade boundary a school will
  land
- And it has essentially never seen enough Inadequate schools to learn
  what they look like

. . .

That is an honest, useful answer - and a far better one than a single
accuracy figure would have given you.

# Categories without an order {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## When there is no natural ordering {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- Ofsted ratings are ordered, so ordinal logistic is the right tool
- But plenty of categorical outcomes are not: which region a school is
  in, which type of school a pupil moves to, which of five clusters a
  neighbourhood falls into
- **Multinomial logistic regression** handles those - it fits a separate
  set of coefficients for every category against a reference

. . .

Let's fit it to Ofsted anyway, *deliberately ignoring the order*, to see
what ignoring the order costs us.

## The comparison {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: hide
library(nnet)
multi <- multinom(
  factor(rating4, ordered = FALSE) ~ P8MEA + PTFSM6CLA1A + PERCTOT +
                  PPERSABS10 + log(TPUP) + PTPRIORHI + MINORGROUP,
  data = train, trace = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
pred_multi <- predict(multi, newdata = test)
acc_multi  <- mean(as.character(pred_multi) == as.character(test$rating4))

tibble(
  Model = c("Ordinal (proportional odds)", "Multinomial"),
  `Parameters` = c(length(coef(ord)) + length(ord$zeta), length(as.vector(coef(multi)))),
  `Test accuracy` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * c(acc_ord, acc_multi)),
  AIC = round(c(AIC(ord), AIC(multi)))
) |> kable()
```

::: incremental
- The multinomial buys about
  **`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (acc_multi - acc_ord))` of a percentage
  point** of accuracy
- It spends **more than twice as many parameters** to get it
- AIC mildly prefers it, which tells us the proportional-odds assumption
  is not perfectly met
:::

. . .

**Use the structure in your data when you have it.** The ordinal model
gets almost the same performance from a third of the coefficients, and
you can actually interpret it.

# Counting things {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## A different kind of outcome {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Let's change the question and move up a level.

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em"}
*How many below-Good schools does each local authority have?*
:::

::: incremental
- That is a **count**: 0, 1, 2, 3... never negative, never fractional
- Most LAs have a few; some have none at all; a couple have a lot
- A straight line will happily predict minus two struggling schools,
  which is not a thing
:::

## What counts look like {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: 95%

la <- schools |>
  group_by(LANAME) |>
  summarise(n_schools = n(),
            n_below   = sum(below_good),
            mean_fsm  = mean(PTFSM6CLA1A, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_abs  = mean(PERCTOT, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_schools >= 5)

ggplot(la, aes(n_below)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = casa_teal, colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Schools rated below Good", y = "Local authorities",
       title = sprintf("%d local authorities; mean %.2f, variance %.2f",
                       nrow(la), mean(la$n_below), var(la$n_below)))
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
Discrete, non-negative, right-skewed, with a pile-up at the low end -
**`r sum(la$n_below == 0)`** LAs have no below-Good schools at all. This
is a Poisson-shaped problem, exactly as week 1 described.
:::

## But first - counts or rates? {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| label: offset-motivate
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
pick <- la |>
  filter(LANAME %in% c("Lancashire", "Bury")) |>
  arrange(desc(n_schools)) |>
  transmute(`Local authority` = LANAME,
            `Secondary schools` = n_schools,
            `Rated below Good` = n_below,
            `As a share` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * n_below / n_schools))
knitr::kable(pick, align = "lrrr")
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**On the raw count, Lancashire looks nearly four times worse.** On the share,
Bury is the one in trouble.

A count on its own tells you very little, because it depends on how many
chances there were to begin with. Lancashire has six times as many schools, so
it would take more below-Good ones even if nothing were wrong.
:::

## So why not just divide? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

The obvious move is to model the share — `n_below / n_schools` — and be done
with it. Two reasons not to:

::: incremental
-   **Poisson describes whole numbers.** `22/79 = 0.28` is not a count of
    anything. We would be using a distribution for something it does not
    describe
-   **Dividing throws away how much evidence you have.** Bury's 46% rests on
    **13** schools. Lancashire's 28% rests on **79**. We should be far more
    confident about Lancashire — but once both are just "a percentage", the
    model can no longer tell them apart
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
An **offset** gets us both: the outcome stays a genuine count, so Poisson
still applies and the sample sizes still count for something — but the model
does the dividing internally.
:::

## What an offset actually is {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Three lines of algebra, and nothing clever happens in any of them.

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**1. What we actually want to model** — a rate, not a count:

$$\log\left(\frac{\text{expected count}}{\text{number of schools}}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x$$

**2. The log of a ratio is a difference of logs** — ordinary school algebra:

$$\log(\text{expected count}) - \log(\text{number of schools}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x$$

**3. Move that term across to the other side:**

$$\log(\text{expected count}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \log(\text{number of schools})$$

That final term — $\log(\text{number of schools})$ — **is the offset**.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
So an offset is just **a division, rewritten as an addition** so it can sit
inside a model that works on the log scale. In R that is
`offset(log(n_schools))`.
:::

## Fixed, not estimated {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Look at line 3 again. Every other term on the right gets a $\beta$ in front of
it that the model **chooses**. The offset does not — it is stuck there with a
coefficient of exactly **1**, because that is how it arrived.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
In plain words, we are **telling** the model something rather than asking it:

> *Twice as many schools, twice as many below-Good ones expected, all else
> being equal.*

That is a claim about arithmetic, not about education policy, so we spend no
parameter finding it out.
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| label: offset-vs-estimated
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
est_m <- glm(n_below ~ mean_abs + log(n_schools), data = la, family = poisson)
ci    <- confint.default(est_m)["log(n_schools)", ]
```

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:10px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
**Is that a fair thing to assume?** Put `log(n_schools)` in as an ordinary
predictor and let the model estimate it instead. It comes back with
**`r sprintf("%.2f", coef(est_m)["log(n_schools)"])`**, with a 95% interval of
`r sprintf("%.2f", ci[1])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", ci[2])` — 1 sits comfortably
inside it. The assumption holds, and fixing it saves us a parameter.

**Always worth checking.** If that interval had excluded 1, the offset would
have been the wrong tool.
:::
## Running a Poisson model {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
pois <- glm(n_below ~ mean_fsm + mean_abs + offset(log(n_schools)),
            data = la, family = poisson)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
pc <- summary(pois)$coefficients
tibble(
  Term = c("(Intercept)", "Mean % disadvantaged", "Mean % absence"),
  Coefficient = round(pc[, 1], 4),
  `Rate ratio` = round(exp(pc[, 1]), 3),
  `p` = ifelse(pc[, 4] < 0.001, "<0.001", as.character(round(pc[, 4], 3)))
) |> kable()
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
The link function here is $\log$, so exponentiating gives a **rate
ratio**. And note the result: once average absence is in the model,
**average disadvantage adds nothing detectable** - a confounding story
of exactly the kind we met in week 6.
:::

## Checking the Poisson assumption {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

The Poisson distribution assumes something quite strong: that the
**variance equals the mean**. Real data often disagrees.

```{r}
#| echo: true
dispersion <- pois$deviance / pois$df.residual
dispersion
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
A value near **1** means the assumption holds. Much above 1 means
**overdispersion** - the data are more variable than Poisson allows,
your standard errors are too small, and you will think results are
significant when they are not.

Here we get **`r sprintf("%.2f", dispersion)`**, which is mild. So
Poisson is adequate - but we should check rather than assume.
:::

## When it is not adequate {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
nb <- MASS::glm.nb(n_below ~ mean_fsm + mean_abs + offset(log(n_schools)), data = la)

tibble(
  Model = c("Poisson", "Negative binomial"),
  AIC = round(c(AIC(pois), AIC(nb))),
  `SE on absence` = sprintf("%.4f", c(summary(pois)$coefficients["mean_abs", 2],
                                      summary(nb)$coefficients["mean_abs", 2]))
) |> kable()
```

- The **negative binomial** is the Poisson's more forgiving cousin - it
  adds a parameter that lets the variance exceed the mean
- This is exactly the distribution we met in week 1, and this is what it
  is for
- Here the two models are essentially tied, so we keep the simpler one

. . .

**Fit the Poisson, check the dispersion, escalate only if you need to.**

## The fun bit: who beats their own odds? {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| out-width: 95%

la <- la |>
  mutate(expected = fitted(pois),
         resid    = (n_below - expected) / sqrt(expected))

plot_la <- bind_rows(
  la |> slice_max(resid, n = 6) |> mutate(grp = "More than expected"),
  la |> slice_min(resid, n = 6) |> mutate(grp = "Fewer than expected")
)

plot_la |>
  pivot_longer(c(n_below, expected), names_to = "what", values_to = "val") |>
  mutate(what = recode(what, n_below = "Observed", expected = "Model expects")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = val, y = fct_reorder(LANAME, resid), colour = what)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = LANAME), colour = "grey70", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3.4) +
  facet_wrap(~grp, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Observed" = casa_red, "Model expects" = casa_teal),
                      name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Schools rated below Good", y = NULL,
       title = "Where the model is wrong, and in which direction") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
Given their intake, some LAs have far **more** struggling schools than
expected and some far **fewer**. The residuals of a count model are not
a diagnostic afterthought here - they are the finding.
:::

# One more outcome type {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Proportions out of a known total {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Back down to school level, and to a file we have not touched yet: **what
happens to pupils after Year 11?**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
dest <- destinations |>
  inner_join(schools, by = "URN") |>
  filter(!is.na(COHORT), COHORT > 0, !is.na(OVERALL_DEST), !is.na(PTFSM6CLA1A)) |>
  mutate(not_sust = COHORT - OVERALL_DEST,
         prop     = OVERALL_DEST / COHORT) |>
  filter(not_sust >= 0)

tibble(
  ` ` = c("Schools", "Median cohort", "Median % sustaining a destination",
          "Schools at exactly 100%"),
  Value = c(comma(nrow(dest)), comma(median(dest$COHORT)),
            sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * median(dest$prop)),
            sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", sum(dest$prop == 1), 100 * mean(dest$prop == 1)))
) |> kable()
```

- Each school gives us "**x** of **n** pupils went on to education,
  employment or training"
- That is not really a percentage - it is a **count out of a known
  total**, which is exactly what the binomial distribution describes

## Modelling it properly {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
dest_glm <- glm(cbind(OVERALL_DEST, not_sust) ~ PTFSM6CLA1A,
                data = dest, family = binomial)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
or10 <- exp(coef(dest_glm)["PTFSM6CLA1A"] * 10)
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em"}
Note the `cbind()` - we hand the model **successes and failures**, not a
proportion, so it knows a school of 30 carries less weight than a school
of 300.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em"}
**Every 10 percentage points more disadvantage is associated with a
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - or10))` fall in the odds of a pupil
sustaining a destination.**
:::

## Does it matter? Compare the predictions {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: 95%

dest_ols <- lm(I(prop * 100) ~ PTFSM6CLA1A, data = dest)
gd <- tibble(PTFSM6CLA1A = seq(0, 100, length.out = 200))
gd$OLS <- predict(dest_ols, newdata = gd)
gd$GLM <- 100 * predict(dest_glm, newdata = gd, type = "response")

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = dest, aes(PTFSM6CLA1A, 100 * prop),
             alpha = 0.10, colour = casa_purple, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = gd, aes(PTFSM6CLA1A, OLS, colour = "Straight line (OLS)"), linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_line(data = gd, aes(PTFSM6CLA1A, GLM, colour = "Binomial GLM"), linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Straight line (OLS)" = casa_red,
                                 "Binomial GLM" = casa_teal), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "% disadvantaged pupils", y = "% sustaining a destination",
       title = "Same data, two models") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
They agree almost exactly through the middle and **diverge at the top
end** - the schools policy cares about most. Here OLS is not obviously
broken. It is quietly wrong at the edges, and **nothing in its output
tells you so**.
:::

## And check the dispersion again {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
disp_dest <- dest_glm$deviance / dest_glm$df.residual
tibble(
  Model = c("LA below-Good counts (Poisson)", "Destinations (binomial)"),
  Dispersion = sprintf("%.2f", c(dispersion, disp_dest)),
  Verdict = c("Mild - Poisson is fine",
              "Overdispersed - use quasibinomial")
) |> kable()
```

. . .

- **Two models, two different answers.** The check is not a formality
  you tick off
- For the destinations model, switching to `family = quasibinomial`
  widens the standard errors by about 60% - the coefficients are
  unchanged, but our confidence in them was overstated

# Wrapping up {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## The family, in one slide {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

| Outcome | `family =` | Link | Interpret coefficients as |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Continuous | `gaussian` | identity | Units of y per unit of x |
| Yes / no | `binomial` | logit | Odds ratios |
| x out of n | `binomial` | logit | Odds ratios |
| Ordered categories | `MASS::polr()` | logit | Odds of being in a higher category |
| Unordered categories | `nnet::multinom()` | logit | Odds vs a reference category |
| Count | `poisson` | log | Rate ratios |
| Overdispersed count | `MASS::glm.nb()` | log | Rate ratios |

. . .

**One framework.** Change the family, change the link, and everything
you learned about building and interpreting a linear model still
applies.

## What carried over, and what didn't {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Still true**

- The recipe: start simple, add complexity that earns its place
- Confounding, mediation, interactions
- Multicollinearity and VIF
- Thinking hard about what belongs in the model
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Different now**

- No R² - use AIC, deviance, or predictive performance
- Coefficients need exponentiating before they mean anything
- Residual plots look strange and need different diagnostics
- Accuracy is a trap on imbalanced outcomes
:::
:::::

## Where you can go next {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- **Generalised additive models (GAMs)** - when the relationship is
  smooth but not a straight line
- **`glmer()`** - the intersection of this week and last week: a GLM
  with random effects, for grouped non-normal data
- **Spatial and geographically weighted regression** - when the
  relationship itself varies over space
- **Ridge and lasso** - when you have too many predictors and need the
  model to choose

. . .

You now have the two big extensions to OLS: last week we relaxed
**independence**, this week we relaxed **normality**. Almost everything
else is a combination of the two.

## Conclusions {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- **Look at your outcome variable before you choose a model.** Week 1's
  data types were not an academic exercise - they determine what you are
  allowed to do
- A GLM is not a new method, it is the same linear predictor with a
  different distribution and a link function bolted on
- **Always compare against a baseline.** A model that beats "predict the
  majority every time" by half a percentage point has not learned much
- Check your assumptions - dispersion for counts, and the threshold
  question for classification
- And ask where your predictors came from. Our best one turned out to be
  something Ofsted had already read

## Today's Practical {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- Building and interpreting your own logistic and Poisson models on the
  schools data
- Practice at the bit that matters most: **interpreting odds ratios and
  rate ratios** in plain English
- And deciding, for an outcome of your own choosing, which member of the
  family you actually need
